rationale: Start with a broad gradient at an intermediate temperature to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. This provides a baseline for targeted changes in gradient slope and temperature.

Change only gradient duration to measure which crowded pairs respond to a shallower slope. The initial run leaves enough time margin to spread the central cluster and late pair without a substantial time penalty.

The shallower gradient resolved most of the crowding but left one nearly coeluting pair. Raising temperature while holding the gradient fixed tests selectivity for that pair and should shorten retention.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 60 C to improve the remaining close pair while retaining the favorable temperature selectivity. The last peak at 8.56 minutes leaves room for this adjustment before the time penalty begins.

The remaining close pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so reverse direction and steepen slightly relative to the best run. This should improve that pair and shorten the run, while testing whether the earlier pairs retain adequate resolution.

The best run is almost fully resolved, so test a small temperature adjustment while preserving its gradient. This probes whether modest selectivity changes can lift the R = 1.46 pair above threshold without compromising the other pairs.

Return to 60 C and raise the starting organic fraction one step, which slightly shallows the gradient while shifting its window. This tests a finer selectivity adjustment between the competing early and late critical pairs than changing duration by two minutes.

Lower the endpoint one step to gently flatten injection 7’s gradient, aiming to resolve its two early close pairs. Its later critical pair has some resolution margin, making this a promising balance between the competing slope responses.

Use a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, between injections 7 and 8, to recover the late pair’s resolution while preserving the early separations. The narrower window still comfortably covers all observed elution fractions and permits this finer slope adjustment on the instrument grid.

Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise the starting organic fraction while keeping the endpoint and duration fixed to test a shorter elution window, with the shallower slope helping offset compression of the early pairs.

Return to the fully resolved starting fraction and test a slightly steeper slope than injection 9 to shorten retention. This small grid-compatible adjustment probes the resolution limit while retaining injection 9 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Injection 9 remains optimal in CRF, and further steepening has reached a resolution limit. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with its gradient unchanged to look for an alternative separation pattern that could support subsequent acceleration.

The low-temperature run has only one unresolved pair, so raise temperature one step with the gradient unchanged to test its selectivity response. If full resolution is recovered, this alternative temperature regime can then be tested with a narrower, faster elution window.

Shift the low-temperature gradient window upward while preserving its slope to shorten retention and test starting-fraction selectivity for the remaining close pair. Injection 9 remains the maximum-CRF benchmark.

Test a steeper gradient in the shifted low-temperature window to move the nearly coeluting pair through its apparent selectivity crossover and shorten retention. This explores a faster alternative while preserving injection 9 as the established maximum-score method.

Raise the starting fraction to test whether the central pair separates further after its observed order reversal. Slightly reduce the slope relative to injection 15 to help the late pair, while the higher starting fraction should shorten retention.

Injection 16 achieves maximum CRF with much shorter retention. Shift its gradient window upward one step at unchanged slope to test further acceleration while monitoring the central cluster and the marginally resolved late pair.

Flatten injection 17’s gradient to recover its two under-resolved pairs while retaining the faster starting fraction. This may achieve full resolution with a last peak earlier than injection 16’s 4.56 minutes.

Test a higher starting fraction with a substantially shallower slope to offset the central-pair compression seen when shifting the window upward. Injection 18 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark; this tests whether another window shift can shorten retention without losing resolution.

Return to injection 18’s fully resolved window and raise temperature one step to test further acceleration through temperature rather than starting fraction. Monitor the central pair closely, since its resolution margin is modest.

The central pair converges as temperature rises from 25 to 30 C; test beyond the likely crossover to see whether it separates again in reversed order. This explores a faster selectivity regime while retaining injection 18 as the fastest fully resolved method.

Return to the fastest fully resolved temperature and starting fraction, then test a slope halfway between injections 18 and 17. This brackets the steepest usable gradient for this window while keeping injection 18 as the fully resolved fallback.

Test whether a shallower slope can rescue the single unresolved pair at the higher starting fraction used in injection 19. Injection 18 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark; this run checks the remaining nearby window before final selection.

The sole unresolved pair at phi0 = 0.40 improves as the slope decreases, so flatten it another step to test for full resolution. This may provide a higher-resolution alternative, while injection 18 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Trim injection 18’s gradient to just beyond its observed elution window while preserving its starting fraction, slope, and temperature. All peaks should still elute during the gradient, retaining maximum CRF and the 4.14-minute last peak while shortening the programmed gradient from 10 to 4 minutes.
